title: Epicurus
keyWorks: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things (1st century BC)
summary: Epicureanism is the school Epicurus founded in Athens around 306 BC; his community met in a garden, and so it came to be called simply “the Garden.” Epicurus taught that the goal of life is pleasure, but he understood pleasure not as luxury and excess, but as peace of mind and freedom from pain. The main ways to it are a sober understanding of nature, a simple life, and friendship.
onEmotions: Epicurus saw philosophy as medicine for the soul: its job is to free us from needless suffering, not to argue for argument's sake. For him, feelings of pleasure and pain are a natural compass given to us by nature, and it is right to listen to them. But many painful experiences, Epicurus believed, grow out of “empty opinions” — false beliefs about the gods, death, wealth, and fame — that inflate our anxieties and desires. The goal is ataraxia: tranquility, a calm clarity of the soul, like a smooth sea without a storm. It is reached not by suppressing feelings, but by understanding which desires are truly our own, and by caring for simple joys.

anxiety.text: Over the gate of Epicurus' Garden, legend says, hung the words: “Stranger, here you will do well to stay.” Here your anxiety would be met with care, not reproach: a living being wants to be safe. Epicurus believed that many of our anxieties grow out of “empty opinions” — beliefs that don't survive a calm examination: that we must earn the favor of higher powers, have more and more, avoid every failure. His followers condensed the teaching into a “fourfold remedy”: most of what we fear is bearable, and what we truly need for a good life is simple and within reach. Epicurus advised returning to the “natural and necessary” needs: food, shelter, friendship, rest. If your anxiety points to these, they deserve your care. But if it has been inflated by empty opinions, you can calmly ask yourself: what do I actually need?
anxiety.practice: Read the four lines of the “fourfold remedy” slowly, aloud: “God is not to be feared. Death is not felt. The good is easy to get. The terrible is easy to endure.” After each one, take a breath and ask: does this touch my worry?

quote.text: Don't fear god, don't worry about death; what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure.
quote.author: Philodemus of Gadara (summarizing the teaching of Epicurus)

fear.text: “As children tremble and fear everything in the blind dark, so we in the daylight sometimes fear things no more terrible,” wrote Lucretius, the Roman disciple of Epicurus. He did not mock fear: your body is protecting you as best it can. But this terror, he said, is dispelled not by the rays of the sun but by understanding how nature works. The Epicureans studied the world — atoms, the causes of things — not out of curiosity, but to free themselves from fear of the unknown. You can accept fear as an invitation to clarity: what exactly scares me, how likely is it, what do I know and what don't I? Often what is seen clearly becomes smaller and easier to bear.
fear.practice: “Turn on the light” literally, as Lucretius would: go to a window or a lamp, look at the ordinary things around you and name three of them aloud. Then, just as calmly, name what you fear in one precise sentence.

sadness.text: “Empty is the argument of the philosopher by which no human suffering is healed,” Epicurus said. So his school approaches sadness like a doctor: gently, practically, and without demanding that you be cheerful all the time. First, it's worth noticing whether there is a real lack behind the sadness — of rest, company, simple pleasures — and gently tending to it. Second, remember that pleasure for Epicurus is not a party or merriment, but above all the absence of needless pain: bread and water, he wrote, give the greatest pleasure to someone who needs them. Epicurus also advised recalling the good things that have been, as a counterweight to present heaviness. You can accept sadness as a quiet signal that your soul needs a little simple warmth.
sadness.practice: Allow yourself five minutes of simple warmth: a blanket, a patch of sun by the window, a hot mug in your hands. Epicurus would say this is no trifle but real pleasure — stay in it without hurrying.

quote.text: Empty is the argument of the philosopher by which no human suffering is healed.
quote.author: Epicurus
quote.source: fragment preserved by Porphyry (Letter to Marcella, 31)

grief.text: Epicurus outlived his closest friend, Metrodorus, and in his will asked the friends to gather every month in memory of them both. His school does not deny the enormous pain of loss: even the wise, the Epicureans admitted, will grieve. But their teaching offers a particular consolation — grateful memory. Epicurus held that the past belongs to us securely: the good we have lived through can never be made not to have been. Loss takes away the future along with the person, but it does not take away what was between you: the conversations, the laughter, the days together. Epicurus wrote that the memory of a friend who has died can be sweet, and advised honoring departed friends not with lamentation but by thinking of them. Grief can be lived through at your own pace, alongside the people who are still here — for Epicurus, friendship was life's main support.
grief.practice: Following the Epicurean memorial gatherings, tell someone — a friend, or simply the air — one story about the person you lost: a particular day, a phrase they used, a funny moment.

quote.text: We should find solace for misfortune in the grateful recollection of what has been lost, and in the knowledge that what has happened cannot be undone.
quote.author: Epicurus

loneliness.text: “Before you consider what to eat and drink, consider whom you will eat and drink with” — Seneca passes on this advice of Epicurus. A school that asked the question this way understands well why loneliness hurts so much. For Epicurus, friendship was not a pleasant extra but one of the chief goods of life. He lived with his friends and students in a community — the Garden — which welcomed women and slaves, a rarity at the time. Your loneliness is the voice of one of the most natural needs there is. Epicureanism suggests that friendship grows from small things — a shared meal, a conversation, mutual support. You don't have to look for deep closeness right away. You can start with one small step toward someone, and remember that needing people is part of what makes you human.
loneliness.practice: Invite one person to share tea, a walk, or at least a phone call with you — a short message, right now. If there is no one to invite, picture at your table someone it would feel easy to be with.

quote.text: Of all the things which wisdom provides for the happiness of the whole of life, by far the greatest is the possession of friendship.
quote.author: Epicurus

anger.text: Philodemus of Gadara, an Epicurean whose library was buried by the ash of Vesuvius, left a treatise On Anger — its charred scrolls are still being read today. Anger flares when something important is touched, and Philodemus took it very seriously. He distinguished “natural anger” — an unavoidable, proportionate response to a real wrong, with nothing shameful in it — from “empty anger,” inflated by false opinions, a thirst for revenge, and endlessly chewing over the injury. Empty anger, he thought, torments the angry person most of all, destroying their peace and their friendships. An Epicurean would suggest asking yourself: how much of my anger is about real harm, and how much about ideas of how things “should” have been? You can accept anger as a signal about your boundaries and tend to them calmly, without handing over your tranquility to it.
anger.practice: Philodemus advised against chewing over an injury. Take ten slow breaths out, and with each one sort it in your mind: “this happened” — “this I am adding.” Then ask yourself which part you can let go.

shame.text: “Live unnoticed” — this short formula of Epicurus sounded like a challenge to a city where fame and the crowd's opinion decided everything. The weight of shame often lives in exactly that gaze of others, and Epicurus counted the chase for approval among the “empty,” insatiable desires. If your shame has grown out of a fear of seeming not successful, attractive, or proper enough, an Epicurean would ask: is that really needed for a happy life? At the same time, the Epicurean community valued frankness among friends — parrhesia, open speech: students shared their mistakes in order to receive support and advice, not condemnation. Philodemus wrote about this. Shame grows lighter when it can be shared with people who wish you well. A mistake spoken aloud in a circle of friends stops being a secret that gnaws at you.
shame.practice: Think of someone who treats you warmly. Imagine telling them, in one sentence, what troubles you — and picture their face as they hear it. For now, that is enough.

guilt.text: For Epicurus, justice begins not in the heavens but with an agreement between people: neither to harm one another nor to be harmed. If guilt is gnawing at you, it means you know how to care for others and keep such agreements. Guilt shows where, as you feel it, this agreement has been broken. The Epicurean response to guilt is practical: admit the mistake, make up for the harm where possible, talk things through — especially with friends, since friendship rests on trust. Endless self-punishment, in this logic, only adds suffering and helps no one. Epicurus wanted to free people from the fear of eternal punishment; an inner trial that never ends is, in essence, much like that fear. You can do everything in your power — and then allow yourself to return to peace.
guilt.practice: Choose one small act that mends the agreement: a one-sentence apology, a debt repaid, a phone call. Do it, or set a time for it — and tell yourself that this trial is over.

envy.text: “Nothing is enough for the one to whom enough is too little,” wrote Epicurus. Envy usually arrives through comparison, and its sting can be very sharp. Epicurus suggested working out what exactly we want. He divided desires into three kinds: natural and necessary (food, shelter, friendship), natural but not necessary (fine food, beautiful things), and “empty” — for example, the desire for boundless wealth or fame. Empty desires have no natural limit, so they can never be satisfied: there will always be someone who has more. Envy often feeds on precisely these. Epicurus reminded us that much of what we already have was once the object of our dreams. You can accept envy as a reason to ask yourself: do I really want this for myself — or have I been hooked by someone else's comparison?
envy.practice: Slowly look around the room and name aloud one thing or one relationship you once dreamed of and now have. Stay with it for three breaths.

quote.text: Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not; remember that what you now have was once among the things you only hoped for.
quote.author: Epicurus

emptiness.text: “The flesh cries out: not to be hungry, not to be thirsty, not to be cold,” wrote Epicurus; whoever has these may rival Zeus himself in happiness. When everything feels hollow and it is hard to want anything, he would probably advise returning to exactly these simplest, “natural and necessary” pleasures. Epicurus stressed that joy does not require big events: a sip of water for the thirsty, warmth for the chilled, rest for the tired — these are already real pleasures. He especially valued calm, “stable” pleasure — the state in which simply nothing hurts. In emptiness, you don't need to force yourself to feel delight. You can start with the body: eat, get warm, get some sleep, spend time near a friend. Epicurean wisdom lies in noticing these small goods while desire and interest slowly return.
emptiness.practice: Drink a glass of water slowly, in small sips — Epicurus counted this a real pleasure for the thirsty. Notice the coolness, the taste, the way your body responds, even if the response is faint.

confusion.text: “The beginning and greatest good of all this is prudence,” Epicurus wrote to Menoeceus — more precious than philosophy itself. When a choice has no clear answer, feeling lost is easy, and prudence is where to begin. His method was “weighing”: comparing not only immediate pleasures and discomforts but their consequences. Some pleasures later bring a lot of pain, and some difficulties lead to a greater good. Epicurus also trusted direct experience: he considered sensations and feelings “criteria of truth,” the starting point of knowledge. When you feel lost it helps not to rush to grand conclusions, but to return to what you clearly feel and know right now. And, in the spirit of the Garden: don't decide important things alone — talk them over with friends. You can accept confusion as a reason for calm reflection, not as a sign that something is wrong with you.
confusion.practice: Go for a short walk — even just around the block — and take only one of the options with you. Ask it the Epicurean question: what will it bring me now, and what a year from now? Save the other option for the next walk.

fatigue.text: Epicurus founded his school not in the noisy agora but in a quiet garden. Exhaustion and burnout are a clear signal from body and soul that they need such a garden too. Epicureanism is one of the few philosophies that put rest right at the center of a good life. Epicurus taught that the highest pleasure is not vivid excitement but aponia and ataraxia: the absence of bodily pain and the tranquility of the soul. He advised freeing oneself from “the prison of everyday affairs and politics” — that is, from the endless race for status and influence. Burnout often means we have spent too long sacrificing natural needs to empty desires — more success, more approval. Rest, for Epicurus, is not laziness but wisdom. You can accept your tiredness as a sign: it's time to bring simple, quiet pleasures back into your life.
fatigue.practice: Give yourself five minutes of Epicurean leisure: sit by a window or in the shade, do nothing and decide nothing. When a thought about chores arrives, answer it: “Later” — and return to rest.

boredom.text: Lucretius describes a Roman bored with his house: he races to his country villa, driving his horses as if it were on fire, yet the moment he crosses the threshold he starts yawning — and hurries back to town. This restlessness can be agonizing, and Lucretius drew it with sympathy, not mockery. So each of us flees from ourselves, Lucretius writes, but there is no running away from yourself. His answer is to understand the nature of things and one's own life. For an Epicurean, boredom is often born of the chase for novelty: empty desires demand ever stronger sensations and are never satisfied. Natural pleasures, on the other hand — food, a walk, a conversation — repeat endlessly and never grow stale for someone who knows how to notice them. You can accept boredom as a signal to turn from hunting for the new to paying attention to the familiar.
boredom.practice: Step outside for five minutes and look at something you have seen hundreds of times: a tree, a streetlamp, the house next door. Find three details you never noticed — Lucretius would look for novelty not in trips but in the eye.

joy.text: “Pleasure is the beginning and end of the blessed life,” Epicurus wrote in his Letter to Menoeceus — and for centuries he was accused of debauchery for it. Your joy is exactly what his school was created for. He saw nothing shameful in rejoicing. But his joy was not a noisy feast. He himself lived very simply, content with bread and water, and jokingly asked a friend to send him a little pot of cheese so that he could treat himself to a lavish dinner whenever he liked. For an Epicurean, the main sources of joy are friendship, conversation, philosophy, a clear mind. Epicureanism also teaches you to savor joy and remember it: the memory of good things is a source of pleasure too. So joy is not frivolity but exactly what life naturally strives for. You can let yourself live it fully.
joy.practice: Tell someone — in your own voice, not an emoji — what made you glad today. In the Epicurean Garden joy was shared at a common table: that is how it also becomes a pleasant memory.

love.text: “Friendship dances around the world, announcing to all of us that we must awaken to blessedness,” wrote Epicurus. His school prized warm attachment very highly, and your tenderness is in good company here. But in honesty, Epicurus and Lucretius were wary of passionate romantic love. In the fourth book of his poem, Lucretius described erotic passion as a source of restlessness, jealousy, and an insatiable craving that brings no peace. The Epicureans feared not tenderness, but love turning into an “empty” desire to possess and to suffer. Friendship based on trust and mutual care, however, seemed to them one of the highest goods. Tenderness is calmest when there is a lot of friendship in it: goodwill, joy in the other's presence, freedom. Love doesn't have to be a storm — it can be a garden.
love.practice: Do something small and friendly for the person you love today, for no reason and with no expectations: bring them tea, send a funny picture, ask how their day went. A garden-love grows from such small things.

gratitude.text: Dying of a painful illness, Epicurus wrote to a friend that this was his “blessed day, and the last of my life”: the pain was severe, but set against it was the joy of his soul in remembering their past conversations. So for the Epicureans gratitude became almost a medicine. Epicurus considered grateful memory of good things one of the most reliable sources of joy: no one can take the past away. An ungrateful soul, he said, makes a person greedy for endless variety — always seeking new pleasures and never satisfied. Gratitude is not politeness but a practice that makes life fuller: it lets you draw again and again on the good that has already been. You can accept it as a quiet wealth that is always with you.
gratitude.practice: Close your eyes and relive one good conversation from the past: where you sat, what was on the table, how the other person's voice sounded. Epicurus comforted himself this way on his last day — try it for just three minutes.

hope.text: “The future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours,” Epicurus wrote to Menoeceus: we should neither count on it as certain nor despair of it. Hope sustains you, and his school gives it a sober, calm shape. Epicurus also reminded us that what matters most for a good life is simple and accessible: a little food, a roof overhead, friends, peace of mind. So Epicurean hope is modest and dependable: it doesn't make happiness depend on big strokes of luck. Everything necessary is easy to obtain, and one can live without the superfluous. You can hope for the best and at the same time find joy in what you already have now — the one doesn't get in the way of the other.
hope.practice: Say two sentences aloud: “I hope for…” and “Right now I already have…” — ending the second with something very simple: a roof, bread, a friend. Epicurean hope stands on the second sentence.

quote.text: We must remember that the future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours, so that we neither count on it as certain to come nor despair of it as certain not to come.
quote.author: Epicurus

nostalgia.text: Epicurus compared someone who has lived well to a ship that has come into harbor: their goods are safely sheltered in grateful memory. A warm sadness for what has passed would have made sense to him. He considered the past a treasury: the good that has been can never be made not to have been, and you can return to it in memory again and again. The bitterness of nostalgia, for an Epicurean, arises when a memory turns into a wish to get back what cannot be got back. The sweetness comes when we simply rejoice that it happened. You can accept nostalgia as an invitation to grateful remembering: not longing for what is lost, but joy that it belongs to your life forever.
nostalgia.practice: Recall a moment you miss and say aloud, like an Epicurean formula: “It happened, and that can never be taken away.” Repeat it three times and notice how the feeling changes.

craving.text: Picture an Epicurean as a gardener sorting desires like beds: what grew from nature, what the wind of habit blew in. The sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong, and Epicurus would not shame you for it. He suggested telling them apart. Some desires are natural and necessary, like hunger or thirst. Others are natural but not necessary. Still others are “empty”: they are born not of nature but of opinion and habit. Epicurus observed that empty desires have no natural limit, so they can never be fully satisfied. He also taught weighing: not every pleasure is worth choosing if greater suffering follows it. Asking yourself this calm question is not a prohibition but a way of caring for yourself. A craving, Epicurus might say, often speaks not in the voice of your nature, but in the voice of a habit layered on top of it.
craving.practice: Do an Epicurean “weighing” in your imagination: picture yourself an hour after giving in to the craving — and an hour after not giving in. Which of the two scenes would you choose for yourself?

quote.text: Of desires, some are natural and others are empty; and of the natural, some are necessary and others natural only.
quote.author: Epicurus

addiction.text: “The greatest fruit of self-sufficiency is freedom,” wrote Epicurus, who for centuries was mistaken for a preacher of pleasure without limits. In his eyes addiction is not a moral failure but a freedom gradually taken away — one that can be won back. The Epicureans distinguished pleasure as movement — “kinetic” pleasure, a flash, excitement — from pleasure as a state — “katastematic” pleasure: being satisfied, at rest, free of anxiety. Addiction can be understood as a life gradually taken over by a single flash, crowding out the calm pleasures of the settled state. Epicurean therapy is not self-flagellation but a gradual return of simple joys. Epicurus considered friendship the main remedy: his Garden was a community where people supported one another. It is easier to break out of the cycle when your people are nearby — and every step toward calm joys brings relief in itself.
addiction.practice: Choose one calm pleasure — a warm meal, a walk, a conversation — and arrange it for yourself today, without hurry. And if you'd like support, you could look for a mutual-help group — your own small “Garden,” where people hold on to one another.

hangover.text: The Epicureans called their philosophy a medicine, and a doctor doesn't scold a patient — he asks where it hurts. The morning after brings both physical heaviness and a “moral” one — anxiety, shame, gaps in memory — and harsh judgment won't help right now. Epicurus taught approaching pleasures with calculation: sometimes we choose a pleasure followed by greater suffering — and that is not a sin but a miscalculation, one you can learn from. In the morning, his thought about pain may also come in handy: the sharpest suffering usually doesn't last long. The Epicureans considered fear and anxious “empty opinions” the chief enemies of tranquility — for example, the certainty that everyone is now judging you. It helps to check them soberly: what actually happened, and what is anxiety filling in? Everything else can wait while you take care of yourself.
hangover.practice: The body first, as an Epicurean doctor would have it: a glass of water, an open window, five slow breaths beside it. Only then name to yourself one thing you know for certain about yesterday, apart from anxiety's guesses.

euphoria.text: Epicurus distinguished two pleasures, like a flash and a steady light: the “kinetic” kind — movement, excitement — and the “katastematic” kind, a calm state when nothing troubles body or soul. Right now you have a bright flash, and he would not want to spoil it: for him pleasure is a natural good, not a cause for shame. He considered the second the deeper one. Euphoria is a classic pleasure of movement: it is wonderful, but short by nature. An Epicurean would live it fully and then gently “land” it — turn it into calm joy and grateful memory. Epicurus believed that the memory of good things itself becomes a source of pleasure. That way the flash leaves behind not emptiness but warmth.
euphoria.practice: Write two lines about what is making you so happy right now and give them an Epicurean title: “For the memory store.” When the high subsides, reread them — that is your grateful memory.

crash.text: Epicurus could live contentedly on bread and water — so every feast was a gift to him, not a support. The drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid night — can be painful: everything around seems colorless. Epicureanism offers a simple explanation. Pleasure as a flash, the “kinetic” kind, ends by its very nature, and if your whole mood was resting on it, a slump follows. But Epicurus pointed to a steadier foundation — “katastematic” pleasure, the quiet state in which nothing hurts and the soul is untroubled. Against the backdrop of fireworks it can't be seen, but it never goes anywhere. A crash is a good time to return to simple things: food, sleep, quiet, a conversation with a friend. Epicurus considered such joys the most accessible — and they are never followed by a sharp comedown.
crash.practice: Pick one “quiet pleasure” from the Epicurean kit — warmth, tea, fresh air, a call to a friend — and allow it to yourself within the hour, without your phone and without asking whether it is “enough.”

panic.text: One of Epicurus' Principal Doctrines says that the sharpest pain does not last long. A wave of panic is genuinely frightening: your heart pounds, your breath catches, it feels as if something terrible is about to happen. It is not your fault that this is happening. Epicurus thought a great deal about how the soul copes with intense bodily sensations. And indeed, a wave of panic typically peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Epicurus advised leaning on the present and on the memory of good things in hard moments: he wrote to a friend that when he was in great bodily distress, he set against it the joy of remembering their past conversations. Support is close at hand: your body, your breath, a familiar voice.
panic.practice: Plant both feet on the floor, feel it holding you, and breathe out longer than you breathe in. With each exhale, call up a friend's face or a warm conversation — as Epicurus did in his hard hour — while the wave recedes.

dread.text: “Where I am, death is not; where death is, I am not” — this is how Epicurus tried to draw the sting from death. The thought of finitude, the question “what is all this for,” weigh heavily, and people were tormented by them long before him. Epicurus considered the fear of death one of the main sources of human anxiety and thought about it a great deal. His argument is simple: death is the absence of sensation, so it cannot be experienced as something terrible. Lucretius added that the eternity before our birth doesn't frighten us in the least. But what matters most is the conclusion Epicurus drew from this: the value of life lies not in endless duration but in its quality. Not in chasing an “eternal meaning,” but in friendship, conversation, and simple joys that are available today. The abyss recedes as you move closer to life itself.
dread.practice: Ask yourself what Epicurus would ask: what would make today good — not eternal, just good? Pick one simple thing — food, time with a friend, a calm thought — and do it within the hour.

quote.text: Death is nothing to us: when we are, death has not come, and when death has come, we are not.
quote.author: Epicurus

fomo.text: While Athens roared in the agora and the theaters, Epicurus dined with his friends in his Garden and did not think he was missing anything. When your feed shows only other people's peaks, the sense of being in the wrong place is exhausting. Epicurus gave advice on this that still sounds almost defiant: “live unnoticed.” He didn't mean hiding from people, but not spending your life chasing fame, status, and a part in every loud event. He considered such desires “empty”: they have no natural limit and can never be satisfied. For an Epicurean, what matters most happens not where it's loudest, but where you feel at peace and your people are near.
fomo.practice: Put your phone down and walk to the nearest place where you feel at ease: a window, a yard, a bench. Stand there a couple of minutes and ask yourself: whom would I like to share this small “garden” with?

quote.author: Epicurus
quote.source: a saying known from Plutarch's treatise Is “Live Unnoticed” a Wise Precept?

sleepless.text: Epicurus advised meditating on his teaching “day and night,” so as never to be troubled, waking or asleep. Thoughts at three in the morning can be darker and louder than daytime ones, and such a night wears you out. Epicurus would have called many of them products of “empty opinions”: at night the mind is especially eager to paint catastrophes, condemnation, a future that hasn't happened yet. He reminded us that the future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours — which means it doesn't need to be settled right now, in the dark. At night you can also use another of his remedies — grateful memory: return to a pleasant memory and relive it in detail. This isn't a fight against insomnia, but a way to make the night a little kinder.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, breathe out slowly and repeat two lines of the “fourfold remedy” in time with your breath: “The good is easy to get… the terrible is easy to endure.” If you like, then relive one good memory in detail.

betrayal.text: “The true friend is neither one who always seeks advantage, nor one who never links friendship with it,” wrote Epicurus, and his Garden rested on trust. When that trust is broken, the wound goes especially deep: the blow came from someone you believed in. For Epicurus this was a very personal subject: he placed friendship above almost everything in life, which means he knew how painful its collapse is. Epicurus believed that friendship begins with mutual benefit but becomes valuable in itself. Betrayal breaks that value, and it is natural to grieve for it. An Epicurean would note that revenge only prolongs anxiety, while the goal is ataraxia, peace of mind. But Epicurus wouldn't demand that you keep trusting either: you can quietly step away, protect yourself, and turn to those who have stayed loyal. One betrayal does not cancel all the friendship there is in your life.
betrayal.practice: Ask one trustworthy person simply to spend some time with you — a walk, a cup of tea — without even telling them what happened. Epicurus would treat you with the presence of friends, not with talk about the betrayer.

jealousy.text: In the fourth book of his poem, Lucretius described romantic obsession with almost clinical precision: the anxiety, the suspicions, the tormenting desire to possess, the jealous reading of every glance and word. This mixture of love, fear, and insecurity is as old as the world, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. The Epicureans distinguished this anxious passion from calm attachment and friendship, which they valued greatly. An Epicurean would say that jealousy is fed by “empty opinions” — pictures painted by the imagination — and it helps to check them soberly. And one more thing: safety in a relationship is built through trust and open conversation, not control. Epicurean ataraxia here is not coldness, but the chance to love without tormenting either yourself or the other person.
jealousy.practice: Divide a page into two columns: what you know for sure — and what your imagination filled in, those “empty opinions.” Then write one honest sentence you could use to start a conversation.

resentment.text: The Epicurean aim is ataraxia, a soul like a sea at rest; an old grudge is like a wind that keeps raising the waves. Such a grudge is heavy, and most often it grew out of a real injustice. Epicurus looked at such feelings practically: what does this experience bring me — peace, or fresh anxiety? The past cannot be made not to have been, but you can relate to it in different ways: reliving the hurt again and again, or consciously directing your memory toward what was good. Letting go of resentment doesn't mean excusing the person who hurt you. It means no longer paying them with your peace. Sometimes a grievance simply needs to be spoken aloud to a close friend — the Epicureans greatly valued frank conversation.
resentment.practice: Sit for three minutes picturing a calm sea. Each time your mind returns to the grievance, gently note: “wind” — and look at the water again, until the waves grow a little lower.

heartbreak.text: “Of all the things wisdom provides for a blessed life, by far the greatest is the possession of friendship,” wrote Epicurus. A breakup turns life upside down, and afterward the heart truly hurts. The Epicureans understood this pain, even though they were wary of passionate love: Lucretius advised against making it the sole center of one's life. But Epicurus left a thought that may help right now: misfortunes are healed by grateful remembrance of what has been. What you lived through together doesn't disappear — it has already happened and will always remain part of your life. Another Epicurean remedy is friendship: Epicurus believed that friends make almost anything bearable. Right now you can let them be near without demanding of yourself that you quickly “pull yourself together.” The pain is not a mistake; in time it can become a quiet memory.
heartbreak.practice: Call one friend today or send them a message — not necessarily about the breakup; you can simply ask how they are. The Epicurean medicine works even through a short conversation.

impostor.text: Philodemus, an Epicurean from Gadara, wrote a treatise On Frank Speech — about how in the Garden students told one another honestly about their slips in order to grow. The fear of being found out any minute is especially familiar to conscientious people. Epicurus believed that many torments grow out of “empty opinions” — for example, the conviction that our worth depends on fame, status, and other people's judgment. He advised against building your life around how you look in others' eyes. Epicurus would likely see impostor syndrome as largely anxiety about reputation rather than about the work itself. Admitting that you don't know something isn't being exposed — it's an ordinary part of learning.
impostor.practice: Tell one trustworthy person — or at least yourself, aloud — one piece of Epicurean frankness: “Here is what I don't know yet.” Notice that the world did not collapse.

self_hatred.text: Imagine walking into the Epicurean Garden and repeating aloud what your inner critic says: Epicurus' friends would most likely exchange glances — that is not how people are spoken to here. If that voice is loud and merciless right now, you deserve kindness, not agreement with it. Epicurus saw philosophy as a healing of the soul, not as one more way to judge yourself. Cruelty toward yourself, for Epicurus, brings you no closer to wisdom or happiness; it only adds suffering that could be avoided. The inner critic largely speaks in the voice of “empty opinions” — other people's yardsticks, demands, the fear of condemnation. Hence a simple question: would you say this to a close friend? If not, perhaps this voice is wrong. You don't have to argue with it all day — you can simply do one kind, simple thing for yourself.
self_hatred.practice: Take one sentence from your inner critic and say it aloud again — the way a close friend from the Garden would: gently, honestly, with care. The Epicureans believed it is friendly speech that heals.

helplessness.text: In Lucretius, atoms fall through the void, and yet sometimes there is a clinamen — a barely perceptible swerve, thanks to which nothing is fully predetermined and living beings have free will. Feeling powerless to change anything is very hard, and there is no need to blame yourself for it. The Epicureans honestly admitted that much is beyond our control, but they invited us to look at what remains. Even in their strict picture of a world made of atoms and void, the Epicureans left room for a small turn. An Epicurean would say that powerlessness before big things doesn't rule out small swerves — simple actions that bring back a little joy and connection. And there are friends: Epicurus said that what we need is not so much their help itself as the confidence that it will be there.
helplessness.practice: Make one tiny “clinamen” today: take a different route, move a cup, send someone two warm words. A small swerve is already not predetermination.

procrastination.text: “We are born once and cannot be born twice, yet you, who are not master of tomorrow, postpone your joy,” Epicurus wrote; life, he added, is wasted in putting off. Being unable to get started doesn't make you a lazy person. But the point of these words is not to drive yourself with a whip. Epicurus was speaking above all of postponed joy: we put off what would make us happier. An Epicurean would ask: has the task become a source of fear — of failure, of judgment, of its sheer size? The “fourfold remedy” reminds us that what is terrible can be endured and the good is within reach. You can start small — and perhaps with something that is pleasant in itself.
procrastination.practice: Find the smallest and most pleasant part of the task and do it in five minutes, setting up an Epicurean pleasure beside it: tea, your favorite music, sunlight on the desk.

uprooted.text: Epicurus knew what it is to lose a home: his family, like other Athenian settlers, was expelled from Samos, and before founding his Garden in Athens he lived in Colophon, Mytilene, and Lampsacus. A move or emigration knocks the ground out from under you, and longing for the old place is natural. He gathered around him people from many places, and his students even included women and slaves, which was rare in that era. For an Epicurean, home is above all not a territory but friendship: a circle of people with whom you share bread and conversation. A new “Garden” can grow in a new place too — gradually, starting with a single meeting.
uprooted.practice: Choose one spot in your new place — a café, a bench, a path — and imagine bringing someone there one day to share a simple meal. Epicurus, too, began his Garden with a patch of land and a few friends.

overload.text: Epicurus kept away from the din of the agora, where every day someone was arguing, shouting, and spreading news. The endless feed, the notifications, the noise — any mind grows tired of it, and irritation is natural here. Epicurus lived without screens, but he had a precise idea about “empty” desires — those with no natural limit. The need to know everything and keep up with every event is largely such a desire: it can never be satisfied, and the more you consume, the more you want. The Epicurean goal is ataraxia, tranquility like a smooth sea without waves. Today's equivalent of the Garden is a time and place without the feed, with simple things in it: a quiet conversation, a walk, a thought followed all the way through.
overload.practice: Give yourself ten minutes of “Garden” without a screen: take your phone to another room, sit by the window, and let your mind fall quiet. If you feel the pull to check the news, simply mark that desire as “empty.”

unreality.text: Lucretius saw the world as a living fabric of things: dust motes in a sunbeam, the smell of the sea, the roughness of stone — for him all of it was reality's direct touch. But sometimes the world, or you yourself, seems unreal, as if behind glass. It is a strange and sometimes frightening experience, and it can be talked about calmly. Epicureanism is one of the most “down-to-earth” philosophies: for Epicurus, everything that exists is made of atoms and void, and sensations serve as the “criterion of truth” — our direct contact with the world. When reality feels faded, it's worth returning to the simplest sensations — warmth, cold, taste, touch. In the essentials they don't deceive: the world is here, and you are in it. You are part of that fabric, even if right now it feels only dimly so.
unreality.practice: Hold something warm or cool in your palm — a stone, a cup, your keys — and feel its weight and surface, as Lucretius would. Then silently name one sound and one smell around you.

awe.text: Lucretius watched dust dancing in a sunbeam and saw an image of atoms forever moving through the void. Awe before the vast or beautiful is one of the deepest experiences, and the Epicureans prized it. Lucretius, the Roman follower of Epicurus, turned his philosophy into a poem, On the Nature of Things, full of wonder: countless worlds being born and dying. The Epicureans wanted to free people from fear of the gods and of menacing celestial phenomena — but not from wonder. On the contrary: understanding nature, for Epicurus, gives pure pleasure, unclouded by superstition. Lucretius confesses that, contemplating the world opened up by Epicurus's reason, he feels at once a divine delight and a sacred shudder. What you feel now is exactly that kind of experience: knowledge and admiration don't compete in it but strengthen each other. You can simply live it, without rushing to explain anything.
awe.practice: Find a beam of light, a patch of sky, or a cloud outside the window and look at it for a minute, naming and explaining nothing. Lucretius would call this the pure pleasure of the nature of things.

relief.text: “The limit of pleasure's magnitude is the removal of all pain,” say Epicurus' Principal Doctrines. The long-awaited exhale you feel now is something he valued especially. For him the highest pleasure is not sharp delight but precisely the absence of pain in the body and anxiety in the soul: aponia and ataraxia. Relief is the moment you feel this directly: the tension is gone, and life itself, free of anxiety, turns out to be pleasant. Epicurus held that once pain is removed, pleasure doesn't grow any further — it only varies. So relief is not a pause before something “real,” but a complete good in its own right. You can savor it and remember it: Epicurus believed that the memory of pleasures you have lived through is a reliable store that helps on hard days. The memory of this relief will later become that kind of support.
relief.practice: Take three long exhales and with each one notice exactly what has let go: shoulders, jaw, thoughts. This is Epicurean aponia — stay in it, adding nothing.

calm.text: The Epicureans pictured happiness as a sea at rest — water smooth all the way to the horizon. What you feel right now is almost the exact name for the goal of their whole philosophy. Ataraxia is Greek for “untroubledness”: a soul without storms. Epicurus considered this state not a dull pause but the deepest and most stable pleasure — the “katastematic” pleasure of a settled state. It requires no luxury: Epicurus himself was content with bread, water, and the company of friends in his Garden. The calm you feel right now is, by Epicurean measure, a real good and not just an absence of events. It doesn't need anything added to it. You can simply notice what creates it, so that you can find your way back to it more often. The Epicureans believed that such simple conditions for calm are within almost everyone's reach.
calm.practice: Write down “your recipe for ataraxia”: which place, which people, which time and activity are helping your calm right now. Fold the note and put it where you'll find it on an unquiet day.

inspiration.text: Epicurus wrote some three hundred books — more than almost any philosopher of antiquity — and believed it is never too early or too late to do philosophy. The living surge, the desire to create and to understand, was evidently something he knew well. The Epicurean joy of knowing is one of the purest: in one of his sayings, Epicurus observes that in other pursuits the fruit comes only at the end, but in philosophy pleasure goes hand in hand with knowing itself. You can let inspiration lead you, without the pressure of “I have to make something great.” Epicurus also thought and wrote among friends, in constant conversation: inspiration grows when it is shared, and brings joy not only to you.
inspiration.practice: Tell your idea to someone who will be glad along with you — over tea or on the phone, like the conversations in the Epicurean Garden. Let the pleasure be in the talk itself, not in a finished result.

schadenfreude.text: “Sweet it is, when winds churn the great sea, to watch from land another's great struggle” — so Lucretius opens the second book of his poem. Not because another's suffering is pleasant, he explains, but because it is pleasant to feel yourself safe. This feeling is awkward to admit, but the Epicureans described it with rare honesty. Schadenfreude often hides relief: “this didn't happen to me.” The Epicureans would add that if your peace feeds on other people's misfortunes, it is fragile, and there is fear or envy hiding in it. True ataraxia, tranquility, needs no comparison. You can accept schadenfreude as a hint: where do I myself feel in danger?
schadenfreude.practice: Picture yourself on Lucretius' shore: a storm, someone else's ship, you on solid ground. Ask: what storm in my own life is this feeling protecting me from? Answer yourself aloud in one sentence.

quote.text: Pleasant it is, when on the great sea the winds trouble the waters, to gaze from the land upon another's great struggle — not because it is a delight that anyone should suffer, but because it is pleasant to see from what troubles you yourself are free.
quote.author: Lucretius
quote.source: On the Nature of Things, II, 1–4

contempt.text: Epicurus' Garden welcomed women and slaves — a rarity among ancient schools, where the “lower” were more often looked down on. Contempt does the opposite: it puts us above others and walls us off, and it is a heavy, cold feeling. The Epicureans built their philosophy on philia, friendship. Epicurus advised keeping away from political struggle and the chase for fame — but that was not contempt for people; it was care for one's own peace. For an Epicurean, contempt is a restless feeling: it makes you constantly compare, watch, and condemn, and so it takes away your tranquility. It helps to ask: what is it protecting? Often there is hurt or fear behind it. You can simply step away from what harms you, without spending your strength on cold arrogance.
contempt.practice: Go for a walk and look at the people you pass simply as possible neighbors in the Garden — no ratings, no comparisons. Notice how much energy is freed when you don't have to pass a verdict.

disgust.text: Epicurus trusted sensations as a first witness that does not lie: for him they were the “criterion of truth,” reporting something real. So an Epicurean would take disgust, that bodily recoil, seriously — it can honestly warn of something harmful. But Epicurus distinguished the sensation itself from the opinion we add to it — and errors, in his view, live in the latter. In his fourth book, Lucretius explained that the same thing seems pleasant to some and repulsive to others because perception depends on the makeup of the body: what is food for one is poison for another. An Epicurean would ask: where is the real warning here, and where is a habitual judgment or someone else's opinion? If the disgust is aimed at yourself, an Epicurean would gently remind you: your body and your mistakes are part of nature, not a verdict.
disgust.practice: Take a few breaths and sort it the Epicurean way: “this is what my body senses” — name it in one word — and “this is what I think about it.” If the disgust is aimed at yourself, ask whose voice the second part speaks in.

revenge.text: Lucretius wrote that Tityos, his liver forever torn by vultures, lives not in the underworld but among us: he is anyone gnawed by their own passions. The wish for revenge can be just such a vulture — strong and understandable. The Epicureans would approach it practically: will revenge bring peace? Epicurus believed that justice arises from an agreement among people neither to harm one another nor to be harmed — its goal is safety, not retribution. Philodemus, in On Anger, classed the thirst for revenge as “empty anger,” inflated by false opinions and tormenting above all the angry person. Revenge demands constantly thinking about the offender, replaying scenes, making plans — handing them your life. The best thing to do with a hurt is to take care of your safety and boundaries, lean on your friends, and take your time back. Your peace is worth more than someone else's punishment.
revenge.practice: Write down one step that protects you and harms no one — an Epicurean “agreement” with yourself about safety. Make it small enough to take this very week.

anger_at_loved.text: An Epicurean hearing about a family quarrel would ask not “who is to blame?” but “who has eaten and slept today?” Anger at the people closest to you — a partner, parents, children — often comes with shame: “how could I snap like that?” Epicurus divided desires into the natural and necessary — food, sleep, rest, safety — and the empty. When the necessary ones go unmet, irritation builds on its own: a hungry, sleep-deprived, worn-out person flares up easily, most often at whoever is nearby. For an Epicurean, many flare-ups at home speak not of a lack of love but of a lack of the most basic things. Epicurus' will provided for his late friends' children and the people of his Garden; caring for those close to you, by his logic, includes caring for yourself. A flare-up is a signal, not a verdict on your love.
anger_at_loved.practice: Check three simple things the Epicurean way: when did I last eat, sleep, get some air? Meet one of these needs within the hour — that, too, is care for the people close to you.

ambivalence.text: Picture Epicurus' scales: on one pan, what a loved one gives you; on the other, what being near them costs. Loving someone and not being able to stand them at once is bewildering. Pleasure and pain were a natural compass for the Epicureans: one and the same person can bring both, and that is not a contradiction but life. In the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus proposes “measuring against one another” — calmly weighing what brings more good and what brings more suffering, without conclusions in the heat of the moment. Sometimes, he writes, it is worth accepting pain for the sake of a greater good, and sometimes turning down a pleasure followed by greater pain. For an Epicurean, mixed feelings are not a cause for shame but material for this kind of sober look. No need to decide the relationship's fate; it's enough to see both sides honestly.
ambivalence.practice: Write two short columns, like the pans of Epicurus' scales: what in this relationship brings joy, and what brings pain. Draw no conclusions — just look at both pans side by side.

guilty_relief.text: An Epicurean would ask plainly: how could the end of long pain not bring relief? And yet relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time often arrives together with shame. For Epicurus, relief is one of the most natural pleasures: the end of pain and a return to peace. He called such pleasures “katastematic” — the calm pleasures of a state in which body and soul are no longer tormented. After long anxiety, caregiving, and sleepless nights, this relief is only to be expected, and it doesn't cancel love. Epicurus advised keeping the memory of those who have gone with gratitude, and considered the memory of past joys a real good. For an Epicurean, relief and love can live side by side: one speaks of how hard it was, the other of how dear it was.
guilty_relief.practice: Recall one bright moment with this person — from the time before things grew heavy — and hold it in memory for a minute, with gratitude. The Epicureans considered such a memory a good that no one can take away.

indifference.text: Epicurus is often imagined as a cold sage, yet his tender letters to friends have come down to us — even one to a child, full of questions and promises of treats. Sometimes something should move you and inside there is only silence, and that can be frightening. The Epicureans strove for ataraxia, untroubledness, but it is not the same as indifference. Epicurus' tranquility was calm, not numbness. An Epicurean would probably note that numbness often sets in after overload: the soul, like a body after pain, seeks rest and switches off what is too much. This is no reason to blame yourself; it may be a natural breathing space. The Epicureans advised returning to simple pleasures — the taste of bread, a sip of water, a conversation with a friend. It is often with the small, the bodily, the concrete that feeling begins to return.
indifference.practice: Choose one simple sensation — the taste of bread, a smell, the warmth of a cup in your palms — and give it a whole minute, as an Epicurean would. Don't expect anything special; just notice.

escape.text: Epicurus himself once “escaped” — not to the ends of the earth but to a garden on the edge of noisy Athens, where friends lived, philosophized, and looked after one another. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — would have made perfect sense to the Epicureans. His advice to “live unnoticed” was a response to the bustle of politics and the race for fame. But they were sober too: Lucretius describes a man dashing between city and country estate, trying to escape himself — and failing. An Epicurean would suggest distinguishing: what am I running from — real pain that can be reduced, or “empty opinions” that will come along with me? Sometimes a change is needed. Sometimes what's needed is a small “Garden” right here — a place and people around whom you can breathe.
escape.practice: Close your eyes and take a walk through your own “Garden” in your mind: where is it, who is there, what are you doing? Then find one small chance to spend time in it this week — even just an hour.

quote.text: We must free ourselves from the prison of everyday affairs and politics.
quote.author: Epicurus

forbidden_attraction.text: In the Epicurean Garden desires were not shamed but examined — calmly, the way a doctor examines a symptom. Being drawn to someone unavailable or “wrong” happens on its own and can be deeply unsettling. Epicurus would approach it without moralizing: desires are natural, and their mere arising is no vice. But he would suggest a question he recommended asking of any desire: what will happen to me if it is fulfilled, and what if it is not? Epicurus divided desires into natural and empty ones and observed that the empty ones grow from imagination and opinion and know no limit. An Epicurean would explore: how much of this attraction is a living person, and how much is an expectation the mind is filling in — a promise of novelty, attention, a different life? This question passes no verdict and makes no decision for you; it only brings back clarity.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write two lines: what you know about this person for certain — and what your imagination has filled in (a promise of novelty, attention, a different life). An Epicurean would simply look at both lines, passing no verdict.

social_anxiety.text: No one gave speeches to a crowd in Epicurus' Garden — people talked at the table, in a small circle of friends. When shyness and fear of being judged turn every conversation into an exam, such a Garden feels especially welcome. Here the Epicureans are perhaps among the most comforting allies. Epicurus never demanded that anyone shine: he advised living unnoticed and not chasing the approval of the crowd, considering that thirst an empty desire that can never be satisfied. For an Epicurean, you don't need everyone to like you: for happiness, a few well-disposed people with whom you feel at ease are enough. The fear of judgment often feeds on the “empty opinion” that everyone is watching and judging. Epicurus would suggest checking it: is that really so? And which of these people do I truly care about impressing?
social_anxiety.practice: Before a get-together, say to yourself under your breath, like an Epicurean formula: “I don't need everyone to like me.” Take three calm breaths out, and in the group find one person you feel at ease with — that is your small Garden.

uncertainty.text: In Lucretius' world, atoms fall through the void and suddenly swerve a little — for no reason, “at no fixed time and at no fixed place.” When no one knows what will happen and the mind paints the worst, this strange picture turns out to help. Lucretius called this swerve the clinamen: there is room for chance in the motion of atoms. The world is not written in advance; the future, in Epicurus's words, is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours. Hence the conclusion: there's no point either in expecting the worst as inevitable or in demanding guarantees from the future. For an Epicurean, the best remedy for the anxiety of the unknown is to lean on what is here now: simple joys, friends, sober reflection. Epicurus was confident that what a good life requires is, as a rule, within reach even in a changing world.
uncertainty.practice: Look around and name aloud three things you definitely have today: a roof, a cup of tea, a friend you can call. The future is not wholly yours — but these three are.

waiting.text: It is easy to picture the Epicurean Garden on a day someone awaits news from the city: the bread is still broken, the conversation still goes on. Waiting — for results, an answer, news — seems to put life on pause, and that wears you out. The Epicureans valued the present very highly. In one of the Vatican Sayings (14), Epicurus reproaches the person who, though not master of tomorrow, postpones joy — while life meanwhile slips away in delay. Waiting easily turns into that kind of postponement: “once I find out, then I'll breathe.” In Epicurean terms, the result is not in your power, but today is. Calm pleasure in simple things — a cup of tea, a walk, a conversation — is, for Epicurus, complete in itself, not something “while we wait.” You can wait and live at the same time. The waiting is the background, not the whole day.
waiting.practice: Name one simple pleasure you've been putting off “until the news comes” — and give it to yourself today, without waiting. Epicurus would call this bringing joy back from the future into the present.

regret.text: “What has been cannot be made not to have been” — for many this is a verdict, but Epicurus proposed using it to heal misfortunes. Regret over what you did or didn't do is a sign that your life matters to you. The Epicureans had a distinctive view of the past: for them it was not only a source of pain but also a treasure. An old man who has lived well, Epicurus wrote, rests as in a harbor, his goods safe in grateful memory: no one can take away the good that has been lived. This is a double lesson: the past can't be changed, so endlessly arguing with it is needless suffering; but the past also holds things worth keeping. You can acknowledge a mistake, take a lesson from it — and turn your attention to the good that also happened and remains yours.
regret.practice: Next to what you regret, write down one good thing from the same period of your life — something that likewise “cannot be made not to have been.” Let both lines be true.

longing.text: Epicurus wrote warm letters to his friends in Lampsacus and looked forward to seeing them — his philosophy rested on friendship and knew separation well. When you miss one particular person, the Epicureans would understand without many words. The Epicurean response to longing is memory. For Epicurus, remembering joyful meetings is not an empty consolation but a real pleasure: according to Diogenes Laertius, during a grave illness he set against his pain the joy of remembering past conversations with a friend. For an Epicurean, longing speaks of the value of a bond, and it can be softened by returning in memory to specific good moments — not to reopen the wound, but to feel their warmth again. A friend remembered with gratitude, in a sense, remains near.
longing.practice: Write this person a short letter, as Epicurus wrote to his friends in Lampsacus — about one good meeting you remember. You don't have to send it.

world_pain.text: During the siege of Athens, when the city went hungry, Epicurus, Plutarch tells us, fed his students on beans, counted out equally. If you are hurting for the world now — wars, injustice, hard news — the Epicureans knew this feeling firsthand. Their answer was not indifference but islands of friendship and care — the Garden, where people supported one another. Epicurus advised keeping away from political struggle for the sake of one's own peace, but not at all away from people: friendship, help, and simple kindness were what mattered most to him. An Epicurean would suggest distinguishing real help from endless immersion in alarming news, which feeds fear but helps no one. You can carry pain for the world while remaining capable of care — and for that, you need to protect your own tranquility too.
world_pain.practice: Do one concrete act of care today — like Epicurus with his beans: feed someone, call someone, help whoever is near. And spend the evening without news — with loved ones or in quiet.

rejection.text: Hearing a “no,” an Epicurean would first ask: what exactly was taken from me — and what remains? When a refusal feels like a verdict on your whole self, it hurts a great deal. The Epicureans would begin: the pain is real, and like all pain it changes and passes. Then they would sort through the “empty opinions” the mind adds to the fact: “nobody needs me,” “it will always be like this.” Epicurus believed that a happy life needs little, and the most important part of that little is friendship. But friendship, as he saw it, doesn't require everyone's approval: a few people with whom you can be yourself are enough. One rejection does not take away your capacity for friendship or close the door to the future. You can let yourself grieve — and then turn toward those who are near and glad to see you.
rejection.practice: Call or send a voice message to one person who is glad to hear from you — just because, for no reason. Epicurus would treat rejection not by arguing with it but with friendship.

abandonment.text: The Epicurean community was more like a net than a single thread: if one strand breaks, the others hold. The fear of being abandoned can live very deep — you want to hold on to someone and get guarantees. The Epicureans understood that most human torment grows out of fear — and they taught taking fears apart. Epicurus would suggest asking: what here is a real threat, and what is an “empty opinion” painted by the imagination? He also insisted that happiness rests not on one person but on a circle of friendship: it was the gaining of friends that he called the greatest of the things wisdom provides for a happy life. The fear of losing one person grows lighter when you have several supports — not instead of that person, but alongside them. Love doesn't weaken because of this; it becomes freer.
abandonment.practice: Draw your Epicurean “net”: a circle in the middle for you, and around it friends, family, colleagues, communities. Mark one strand you'd like to strengthen, and think about how to see that person.

unrequited.text: Lucretius noticed that a lover sees the beloved through a golden haze: a swarthy girl becomes “honey-colored,” a silent one “modest,” and there is no flaw he won't call a virtue. Love without an answer is a pain as old as the world. The Epicureans, to be honest, were wary of passionate love: Lucretius described it as a thirst that flares up precisely because it cannot be quenched. But the golden haze also holds a consolation. This is not a reproach to you but an explanation of why it hurts so much: you are longing not only for a person but also for an image your heart has created. You can respect your feeling and at the same time gradually turn your attention back to bonds where there is reciprocity — to friendship, to people around whom you feel at ease and warm.
unrequited.practice: Give a little attention today to someone whose warmth is mutual — a friend, a sister, a neighbor: a short visit or a simple “how are you?” The Epicureans treated the unrequited with the reciprocity of friendship.

humiliation.text: In his lifetime Epicurus was showered with slander — rivals invented scandals about him — yet he went on living in his Garden among friends. Humiliation burns: it feels as if you've been stripped of your dignity. The Epicureans would respond with their key question: what in what happened actually harms you, and what is opinion? Epicurus considered the chase for honor and status one of the “empty” desires that are never satisfied. So losing face in others' eyes, painful as it is, does not take away what you need for happiness: friendship, simple joys, a clear mind. The less your peace depends on other people's judgment, the less power those who try to humiliate you have. This doesn't mean the pain should be denied: it is real. But you can gather around it the things that hold you up — above all, people who treat you with warmth.
humiliation.practice: Write down three things you still have after this episode that no mockery can touch: your friends, your skills, your values. The Epicureans would call these what happiness really needs.

body_shame.text: Epicurus measured the body's good not by the mirror but by how it feels: does it hurt, is it warm, is it at ease? Being unhappy with your body is a common, quiet pain. For Epicurus, the body's chief good is freedom from suffering — aponia — and a calm, living sense of well-being, not conformity to some standard. He would probably have counted the pursuit of an ideal appearance among the “empty” desires: they grow out of other people's opinions, know no limit, and bring no peace. For an Epicurean, the body is not a shop window but your home, in which you can experience simple joys: the warmth of the sun, the coolness of the wind, the pleasant tiredness after a walk. The more attention you pay to how your body feels good, the less power the thought of how it “should” look will have.
body_shame.practice: Find one simple bodily pleasure by Epicurus' measure right now — warm water on your hands, a comfortable position, a sip of tea — and stay in it for a minute, asking your body not “how do you look?” but “how are you?”

quote.text: Everything natural is easy to obtain, and only what is empty is hard to get.
quote.author: Epicurus

illness.text: Even while dying of a painful illness, Epicurus wrote to his friends and asked them to look after Metrodorus' children. He knew firsthand how frightening and hard it is when your body lets you down — so his philosophy is not the consolation of a healthy person. He didn't demand that one suffer in silence and didn't shame anyone for weakness; he advised setting against pain what remains good: the joy of friendship, the memory of pleasant conversations, clarity of thought. His friends visited him, and caring for one another was part of Epicurean life. Illness is not your fault and no reason to give up the joys that are still available. Even on hard days you can find small islands of peace and let others take care of you.
illness.practice: Allow yourself one small island of peace today — favorite music, a call to a friend, a pleasant memory — without guilt. Epicurus set exactly such islands against pain.

pride.text: Epicurus called himself self-taught and was not shy about being proud of it, though his rivals mocked him more than once. Your pride is a good, well-earned feeling: for an Epicurean, joy in your own work is one of the purest kinds. Epicurus distinguished pleasure that depends on others' recognition — he considered the chase for fame an empty desire — from the calm pleasure of something done well and in keeping with your values. The first is insatiable; the second is complete in itself. He also valued joy shared with friends: it's nice to celebrate a good piece of work among people who will be glad along with you. Healthy pride doesn't need an audience — you yourself are enough, and perhaps a couple of people close to you.
pride.practice: Throw yourself a small Epicurean celebration: a cup of good tea or a piece of cheese — and one person you can tell about what you pulled off. No bigger audience is needed.

melancholy.text: Lucretius, for all the rationality of his poem, is one of the most melancholy poets of antiquity: everything in it is born and falls apart, atoms come together again in new forms, and there is a remarkable calm in that cycle. A bright sadness, sorrow mixed with tenderness, would have been close to him. Epicurus considered the memory of past joys a real pleasure, and bright sadness often resembles it: it remembers the good while knowing it has passed. For an Epicurean, such sadness doesn't disturb tranquility — it can be a quiet form of it. There's no need to chase it away; you can let it be, like the cool of evening after a hot day.
melancholy.practice: In the evening, step onto a balcony or go to a window and watch the light change for a minute — as Lucretius watched the eternal motion of things. Let the sadness stay with you, like the cool of the evening.
